description: Philippines pathway following National Renewable Energy Plan with some offshore wind development.
pathwayDescription:
The Clean Energy Scenario 1 (CES1) is an explorative power sector pathway for the Philippines developed by the Philippines Department of Energy (DoE) that builds on the assumptions of the Reference scenario. The Pathway includes the National Renewable Energy Program’s (NREP) power generation mix target of 50% renewable energy by 2040, and adds expanded build out of renewable energy capacity through 2050, including a major tranche of 19 GW of offshore wind capacity. Nuclear capacity is added to the grid and the lifetime of coal power plants is capped.

The CES 1 pathway makes strong socio-economic assumptions, with annual real GDP growth averaging well over 6% until 2050 driving significant increases in energy demand. As a result, emissions continue to grow, although at a significantly lower rate than in the DoE’s Reference scenario. Coal generation quickly plateaus, while natural gas and oil consumption continue to rise, driven by industry, transport, and other end-use sectors.

coreDrivers.policies: Wider, more binding instruments than REF drive supply and demand. Technology shares: >50% RE in generation by 2050 under NREP targets. New vs REF: 19 GW offshore wind by 2050 (awarded contracts); nuclear 1.2 GW by 2032, 2.4 GW by 2035, 4.8 GW by 2050. A 40-year coal plant life is a retirement rule, removing 3,600 MW. Tighter demand standards: 5% biodiesel from 2026, 50% EV penetration by 2040, 10% energy savings on oil products and electricity in 2040-2050 via more efficiency.
coreDrivers.technologyCosts: Unit costs drive the build as in REF, using the same 2022 National Renewable Energy Laboratory database and fuel costs, but the signal is more visible given the larger renewable share: the RE capital cost learning curve keeps blended generation rate growth well below REF. Costs also shape the renewable mix within the RE target, with solar and onshore wind ending below REF levels as offshore wind displaces some lower-capacity-factor capacity. Nuclear is an exogenous assumption, not cost-driven.
coreDrivers.investmentChange: Low-carbon investment takes a larger share of GDP than in REF, though it still declines over time as capital costs fall. Total investment is roughly two fifths above REF, with the increase concentrated in renewables, a sharp rise in battery storage, nuclear and other technologies absent from REF, and electric vehicles, the largest single component.
coreDrivers.macroeconomicDrivers: The macroeconomic and socioeconomic assumptions are identical to REF and CES 2 and are recorded for that reason, not as a differentiator: sustained high real GDP growth, with sectoral and household income growth and population as demand predictors, sourced from the Philippine Development Plan 2023-2028 and AmBisyon Natin 2040. Unlike in REF, they do not dominate: policy targets and technology costs shape outcomes, and demand differs from REF through efficiency and electrification, not growth.
coreDrivers.behavioralShifts: The household fuel preference shift from REF also applies, and the publication adds a behavioural element specific to the clean energy case: stronger efficiency and conservation yielding savings on oil products and electricity after 2040. Traditional biomass still declines, with LPG and electricity covering most household demand by 2050. Transport shows the largest cut against REF as alternative fuels displace gasoline and diesel, though EV uptake is a policy target, not a consumer preference.
coreDrivers.otherDrivers: REF’s Competitive Renewable Energy Zone, service contract, reserve margin and network limits apply; two more appear. Offshore wind is sited by grid per the World Bank roadmap, fixing its transmission and balancing needs. Nuclear relies on an institutional programme, not a market: the Philippine Nuclear Energy Program pursues IAEA milestones while nuclear legislation is drafted, so its build rests on a pre-commercial framework. Both are siting and readiness conditions, not instruments or costs.

dependencies.dependency_description: Every increment over REF is policy-delivered, so the pathway is infeasible as modelled without it. Four assumptions are decisive: the RE share target under National Renewable Energy Program goals, awarded offshore wind contracts sited per the World Bank roadmap, staged nuclear capacity, and a coal technical-life rule, the only instrument removing high-carbon capacity. Demand-side EV penetration and B5 blending are equally policy-set. Hydrogen is an ambition with no deployment target.

Two conditions merely important in REF become preconditions. Nuclear needs a framework not yet in place: the Philippine Nuclear Energy Program is meeting IAEA milestones, legislation is drafted but not enacted, and an independent regulator, safeguards and waste regime must precede early operation. Permitting and right-of-way must support a far larger build, and offshore wind needs a marine consenting regime still in development. Storage and ancillary service rules matter more.

The economics work out better than in REF: the RE capital cost learning curve keeps blended generation rate growth well below REF, so the larger clean build avoids a steeper price path. Financing needs are materially larger, though, and shift toward battery storage and nuclear, with weak commercial precedent and no established remuneration model, carbon price or green premium. Transition finance is addressed at plan level via the Philippine Sustainable Finance Roadmap, not as a quantified gap.

Nuclear changes this dependency from REF, and acceptance becomes a programme requirement. The Philippine Nuclear Energy Program lists public information, stakeholder involvement and Nuclear Energy Awareness Training as IAEA infrastructure issues, recognising the need for social licence, with the mothballed Bataan plant as backdrop. Small modular reactors may deploy faster given a smaller footprint. Offshore wind raises coastal and fisheries interests; solar relies on host-community benefits.

Unlike REF, the pathway depends on consumers changing what they buy, not only how they pay for electricity. EV penetration and post-2040 energy savings require mass uptake by households and firms, and deliver the demand-side gap against REF, cutting transport energy use and raising transport electricity demand. With prices more favourable than REF, exposure shifts from willingness to pay to vehicle purchases and sustained efficiency, treated as policy-driven with no adoption-risk assumption.

The same network carries a far harder job than in REF, and the outputs show the cost: variable renewables rise and battery storage reaches several times REF, with grid stability requiring steep storage growth. Offshore wind needs port, marine and dedicated transmission capability, yet its quoted levelised cost omits transmission, an explicit gap. Nuclear adds siting, cooling and fuel-cycle logistics without domestic precedent. Right-of-way and permitting still bind transmission delivery.

Three not-yet-market-ready technologies carry this pathway, against REF’s one. Battery storage must scale far beyond REF, shifting from ancillary service to bulk balancing. Small modular reactors, the route to nuclear, promise faster deployment and lower fuel needs than pressurised water reactors but would be a national first. Green hydrogen is named for firming, storage and offshore-wind-linked production, but lacks volume or date, so it is expected, not modelled. Mature ones are excluded.

Relative to REF, the land and site constraint tightens while import dependence eases. Competitive Renewable Energy Zone potential and awarded service contracts cap RE by grid, and larger additions press harder on it, with offshore wind confined to awarded areas. Lower coal generation cuts coal import exposure, though domestic output still falls. New dependencies arise in nuclear fuel, with no domestic supply chain and addressed via enrichment interest and cooperation, and critical minerals.

Resilience needs match REF in kind but exposure is larger, with two specific dependencies. Offshore wind puts assets in the typhoon belt, engaging climate-proofing and disaster risk financing, insurance and contingency frameworks. Nuclear siting adds environmental and safety needs, with research on small modular reactor protection and monitoring. Waste grows: end-of-life policy is flagged for renewable equipment and batteries, amid larger solar, storage and EV fleets, and radioactive waste.

The skills requirement far exceeds REF’s and extends into occupations the country lacks. Jobs are well above REF, led by renewable plant construction, with sharp rises in storage and EVs and a new nuclear line. Nuclear needs a workforce built from nothing; the Philippine Nuclear Energy Program names human resource development as an infrastructure issue alongside regulation. The publication responds with rightskilling led by the Department of Energy and the Department of Labor and Employment.

byMetric.scopeLimitations: Derived, not published: GHG / generation. Numerator is Transformation-sector GHG, which bundles refining and own-use with power generation, so the result runs about 1.5 percent above a power-only figure - 2022 check 77.44/111.52 = 0.694 against power-only 0.684 and the 0.68 tCO2e/MWh the publication states. Scope 1 combustion only, CO2e on the Kyoto basket. Excludes network losses. 2050 value 0.166 tCO2e/MWh.

Transformation sector, which is power generation plus refining and own use - about 1.5 percent wider than power alone at the 2022 baseline. Scope 1 combustion, CO2e on the Kyoto basket via LEAP IPCC GWP-100. Energy-sector emissions only: no land use, no industrial process emissions. Values 77.44 MtCO2e (2022) to 73.55 MtCO2e (2050).

On-grid capacity across the Luzon, Visayas and Mindanao networks, from the PLEXOS expansion. Energy storage covers battery storage and pumped hydro but is reported as one BESS figure in Volume I with pumped hydro inside the hydro line. Only Power Development Plan 2023-2050 splits battery from pumped hydro - so the two are not distinguishable in the annual series. No reported series for rooftop and behind-the-meter solar, nor for captive industrial generation.

Gross generation, on-grid, across the three modelled networks. Gross rather than net, so station own-use is included and network losses are not netted off. BESS throughput is reported alongside but excluded from the generation total. Total rises from 111.52 TWh (2022) to 443.90 TWh (2050). Hourly dispatch underlies the annual figures but is not published.

Shares of gross generation, on-grid, three modelled networks - so the same boundary as Generation, including station own-use and excluding BESS throughput from the denominator. RE share moves from 22.13 percent (2022) to 64.86 percent (2050). Capacity shares are also published and differ from generation shares; the two should not be conflated.

PhP billion at 2022 prices, converted at PhP55/USD. Two periods only, 2023-2028 and 2029-2050, not an annual series. The renewables line is an aggregate and is not split by individual RE technology, so solar, wind, hydro, geothermal and biomass investment cannot be separated - a material limitation given that renewables are the largest component. No transmission or distribution investment is included. Covers new build; maintenance and refurbishment treatment is not stated.

granularity: High-carbon assets lifetime face early retirement policy
byMetric.scopeLimitations: Applies to coal-fired capacity. A 40-year technical life retires 3,600 MW over 2023-2050, taking coal capacity to 11,111 MW by 2050. The publication describes the retirement as voluntary with possible repurposing rather than mandated, so it is a lifetime rule with an assumed uptake, not a legislated phaseout. No plant-level retirement schedule, vintage profile or repurposing pathway is published, and no lifetime assumption is stated for oil or gas assets.
